The exclusion restrictions that identify wages in the participation equation are: (i) hospital availability in the municipality (affects employment opportunities but not productivity), (ii) availability of kindergarten (affects the cost of work but is assumed not to directly affect wages), and (iii) the local participation rate (a proxy for labour market tightness).

The negative coefficient on "children < 3 years" confirms the expected finding that young children significantly reduce the probability of participation — consistent with the literature on maternal labour supply. The positive coefficient on "hospital in municipality" reflects the availability of nearby nursing jobs.

The Hausman test comparing weighted and unweighted (kernel bandwidth $h = 1$) conditional logit estimates yields $\chi^2_{23} = 821.27$, clearly rejecting the null hypothesis of no sample selection. This justifies the Kyriazidou two-step approach.
:::

## Step 2 — Hours Equation and Lessons

**Kyriazidou (1997) IV estimates** (Table 11.2 — selected coefficients):

| Variable | Estimate | Std. Error |
|---|---|---|
| Ln wage | 0.208\* | (0.094) |
| Shift work | −0.011\*\* | (0.001) |
| Hour 35.5 contract | −0.040\*\* | (0.005) |
| Disabled | −0.258\*\* | (0.026) |
| Single | 0.021\*\* | (0.004) |
| Children $< 3$ years | −0.050\*\* | (0.003) |

\*\* Significant at 1%; \* at 5%. $N = 121{,}622$. **Wage elasticity $= 0.21$** after corrections.

. . .

**Methodological lesson:** The panel structure is essential — simultaneous FE, selection correction, and IV are only feasible with repeated observations of the same individuals.

::: {.notes}
The wage elasticity of 0.21 means that a 10% increase in the offered wage increases hours worked by approximately 2.1%, holding other factors constant and correcting for both sample selection and endogeneity. This is a relatively modest but precisely estimated elasticity.

Comparison: OLS without correction gives a lower elasticity, suggesting that the selection and endogeneity corrections increase the estimated wage effect. Nurses who work are positively selected on productivity (they have higher wages AND work more hours), and ignoring this would give an upward-biased OLS estimate. The IV correction for endogeneity also changes the estimate.

The significant negative coefficient on "shift work" indicates that nurses working irregular shifts supply fewer hours (conditional on the wage), possibly reflecting non-wage compensation differentials.

This application illustrates the full complexity of panel GLM estimation in practice. Each of the three corrections (heterogeneity, selection, endogeneity) requires a different econometric tool, and all three must be applied simultaneously to get consistent estimates. The finding that the wage elasticity is 0.21 after all corrections suggests a meaningful labour supply response among Norwegian nurses.
:::


# Computing Panel GLMs in Stata and R {background-color="#1a2a4a"}

## Architecture: Command Reference Table

| Model | FE Estimator | RE Estimator |
|---|---|---|
| **Binary logit** | `xtlogit, fe` / `clogit` | `xtlogit, re` |
| **Binary probit** | — (no FE probit) | `xtprobit, re` |
| **Ordered logit/probit** | `buc` (SSC) | `xtoprobit` |
| **Poisson count** | `xtpoisson, fe` | `xtpoisson, re` |
| **Negative binomial** | `xtnbreg, fe`\* | `xtnbreg, re` |
| **Tobit (censored)** | — (use Honoré) | `xttobit` |
| **Sample selection** | Kyriazidou `honor` | Heckman + panel |

\**Use with caution — as explained in Panel Count Models*

**R:** `fixest::feglm()`, `pglm::pglm()`, `lme4::glmer()`, `ordinal::clmm()`, `fixest::fepois()`

::: {.notes}
This table provides a quick reference for the main panel GLM estimators in Stata and R. Note that several FE entries are blank or marked with caveats: (1) there is no standard FE probit because the normal distribution does not have a sufficient statistic for $\mu_i$; (2) the FE Tobit requires the Honoré (1992) trimmed estimator rather than MLE; (3) the FE negative binomial in Stata (`xtnbreg, fe`) does not fully control for individual effects in the usual sense (see Allison & Waterman 2002).

For practitioners: the default should be FE Poisson for count data (with robust SEs), correlated RE probit with Mundlak device for binary data, and RE ordered probit with Mundlak device for ordered data. The FE estimators (conditional logit, BUC) are used when the assumption of independence between $\mu_i$ and $x_{it}$ is untenable and one is willing to pay the cost of discarding non-switchers.
:::

## Binary Outcomes — Stata

**Fixed effects (conditional logit):**

```stata
xtlogit y x1 x2 i.year, fe vce(cluster id)
clogit y x1 x2 i.year, group(id) vce(cluster id)
```

**Random effects probit with Mundlak device:**

```stata
bysort id: egen xbar1 = mean(x1)
bysort id: egen xbar2 = mean(x2)
xtprobit y x1 x2 i.year xbar1 xbar2, re intpoints(24)

* Test H0: corr(mu_i, x_it) = 0
test xbar1 xbar2
```

**Post-estimation average partial effects:**

```stata
margins, dydx(*) predict(pu0)
```

::: {.notes}
The `vce(cluster id)` option is essential in all panel GLM estimations — it accounts for within-individual correlation of errors across time periods that is not fully modeled by the individual effects. Standard errors without clustering understate the true uncertainty.

The `intpoints(24)` option in `xtprobit` increases the number of Gauss-Hermite quadrature points from the default 12 to 24, which improves accuracy when $\sigma_\mu$ is large. For most applications, 24 points are sufficient; if `xttest0` (the test for $\sigma_\mu^2 = 0$) is rejected strongly, increase to 32 or higher.

The `predict(pu0)` option computes probabilities setting individual effects to zero — useful for population average marginal effects. For conditional marginal effects (conditional on the individual's $\mu_i$), use `predict(xb)` and then compute $\Phi(\hat{x}_{it}'\hat{\beta})$ manually.

For the Mundlak test: rejection of $H_0: \delta = 0$ suggests that the RE assumption is violated and correlated RE or FE is needed.
:::

## Binary Outcomes — R

**Fixed effects conditional logit:**

```r
library(survival)
clogit(y ~ x1 + x2 + factor(year) + strata(id), data = df)

# Or with fixest (faster for large datasets)
library(fixest)
feglm(y ~ x1 + x2 | id + year, family = binomial, data = df)
```

**Random effects probit with Mundlak device:**

```r
library(lme4)
df$xbar1 <- ave(df$x1, df$id)
df$xbar2 <- ave(df$x2, df$id)

glmer(y ~ x1 + x2 + xbar1 + xbar2 + (1|id),
      family = binomial(link = "probit"),
      data = df, nAGQ = 24)
```

**Average partial effects:**

```r
library(marginaleffects)
avg_slopes(model, variables = c("x1", "x2"))
```

::: {.notes}
For large datasets, `fixest::feglm()` is substantially faster than `survival::clogit()` and provides cluster-robust standard errors through the `vcov = ~ id` argument. It also handles multiple high-dimensional fixed effects (e.g., `| id + year + region`) efficiently.

For `lme4::glmer()`, the `nAGQ` argument controls the number of adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature points. The default `nAGQ = 1` uses Laplace approximation, which is fast but may be inaccurate. `nAGQ = 24` provides good accuracy at the cost of some computation time. Convergence warnings from `glmer()` should be taken seriously — they often indicate numerical problems that can be addressed by scaling variables or increasing the number of optimizer iterations.

The `marginaleffects` package (Arel-Bundock et al. 2024) provides a unified interface for computing marginal effects from virtually any R model object. `avg_slopes()` computes average marginal effects (AME), averaging over the empirical distribution of all other covariates. For probit models, these are the standard "average partial effects" reported in most applied papers.
:::

## Ordinal Outcomes — Stata and R

**Stata — RE ordered probit:**

```stata
xtoprobit y x1 x2 i.year xbar1 xbar2, intpoints(24)
margins, predict(pr outcome(1)) predict(pr outcome(2)) ///
         predict(pr outcome(3)) dydx(x1)
```

**Stata — FE ordered logit (BUC):**

```stata
ssc install buc
buc y x1 x2, group(id) vce(cluster id)
```

. . .

**R — RE ordered probit:**

```r
library(ordinal)
mod <- clmm(ordered(y) ~ x1 + x2 + xbar1 + xbar2 + (1|id),
            link = "probit", nAGQ = 24, data = df)
avg_slopes(mod, type = "cum.prob")
```

**R — Generalised ordered logit:**

```r
VGAM::vglm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = cumulative(parallel = FALSE))
```

::: {.notes}
The `buc` command in Stata implements the Baetschmann-Staub-Winkelmann (2015) estimator. It automatically creates the $J-1$ binary datasets, estimates conditional logit on each, stacks them, and computes cluster-robust standard errors. The `group(id)` option specifies the panel identifier.

In R, `ordinal::clmm()` fits cumulative link mixed models, which include RE ordered probit/logit as special cases. The formula `ordered(y) ~ x1 + x2 + (1|id)` specifies a random intercept model. The `link = "probit"` argument selects the probit link; `link = "logistic"` gives ordered logit.

For the Mundlak device: add `xbar1 + xbar2` to the formula before `(1|id)`. For the dynamic extension: add `lag_y_cat2 + lag_y_cat3 + lag_y_cat4 + y0_cat2 + y0_cat3 + y0_cat4` as additional regressors.
:::

## Count Outcomes — Stata and R

**Stata — FE Poisson (recommended default):**

```stata
xtpoisson y x1 x2 i.year, fe vce(cluster id)
xttest0  // Test H0: sigma_mu = 0
```

**Stata — RE Poisson with overdispersion test:**

```stata
xtpoisson y x1 x2, re
estimates store poisson_re
xtnbreg y x1 x2, re
lrtest poisson_re .  // One-sided test at boundary
```

. . .

**R — FE Poisson with `fixest` (fastest):**

```r
library(fixest)
mod_fe <- fepois(y ~ x1 + x2 | id + year,
                 vcov = ~ id, data = df)
```

**R — Dynamic count with INGARCH:**

```r
library(tscount)
tsglm(y_i, model = list(past_obs = 1, past_mean = 1),
      distr = "nbinom")
```

::: {.notes}
The key message for practitioners: `xtpoisson, fe` with `vce(cluster id)` is the recommended default for panel count data. It is consistent under mild assumptions (correct conditional mean specification), robust to overdispersion (Wooldridge 1999), and computationally efficient.

The `xtnbreg, fe` command in Stata should be used with caution due to the Allison-Waterman (2002) critique. If FE NB is needed, the researcher should verify that the fixed effects are being absorbed through the mean (not the overdispersion parameter). One way to check: compare results from `xtnbreg, fe` with those from `xtpoisson, fe` — if they are substantially different, investigate whether the NB FE is identifying what you think it is.

`fixest::fepois()` is the fastest available implementation of FE Poisson for large datasets. It handles multiple fixed effects (e.g., `| id + year + region`) through the alternating projections algorithm, making it feasible even for millions of observations.
:::

## Censored, Truncated, and Sample Selection — Stata and R

**RE Tobit (Stata):**

```stata
xttobit y x1 x2 i.year, ll(0) vce(cluster id)
margins, dydx(*) predict(e(0,.))
```

**Honoré (1992) FE Tobit (Stata):**

```stata
ssc install honor
honor y x1 x2, model(tobit) ll(0) group(id)
```

**RE Tobit (R):**

```r
library(censReg)
censReg(y ~ x1 + x2, left = 0, data = df)
```

. . .

**Wooldridge (1995) selection test (Stata):**

```stata
probit s z1 z2 x1 x2 if year == t
predict lambda_t, hazard
xtreg y x1 x2 lambda_t_demeaned, fe vce(cluster id)
test lambda_t_demeaned
```

::: {.notes}
The `censReg` package in R provides a maximum likelihood estimator for the random effects Tobit model via the `censReg()` function. The `left = 0` argument specifies left-censoring at zero (the standard Tobit specification). The package also supports right-censoring and double-censoring.

The Honoré (1992) estimator requires the `honor` command in Stata (community-contributed, available from SSC). It implements the trimmed LAD estimator for the FE Tobit model. The `ll(0)` argument specifies the lower limit of censoring.

For the Wooldridge (1995) variable addition test: the demeaned inverse Mills ratio $\tilde{\lambda}_{it} = \hat{\lambda}_{it} - \bar{\hat{\lambda}}_i$ is the key test variable. If the coefficient of $\tilde{\lambda}_{it}$ is significantly different from zero in the FE regression, it suggests nonignorable selection bias.
:::

## Workflow, Diagnostics, and Common Pitfalls

**Step 1 — Test for individual effects:**

```stata
xttest0     // LM test H0: sigma_mu = 0
hausman fe re, sigmamore  // FE vs RE Hausman
```

**Step 2 — Test for serial correlation:**

```stata
xtserial y x1 x2  // Wooldridge test (install via SSC)
```

**Step 3 — Test for selection (if unbalanced):**

```stata
* Wooldridge (1995) variable addition test
* or compare Within and GLS on balanced vs unbalanced
```

. . .

**Common pitfalls:**

- Not clustering SEs at the individual level
- Using `xtnbreg, fe` without understanding the Allison-Waterman caveat
- Ignoring non-switchers in FE logit (check: how many?)
- Running `xttobit` when censoring fraction is high ($> 30\%$)
- Reporting raw $\hat{\beta}$ coefficients without average partial effects

::: {.notes}
The workflow described here is a practical guide for applied researchers. The key diagnostic tests are:

1. `xttest0` (after `xtreg` or `xtprobit/xtpoisson, re`): Tests $H_0: \sigma_\mu^2 = 0$. If not rejected, pooled estimation is consistent.
2. Hausman test: Tests $H_0: E[\mu_i | x_{it}] = 0$. If rejected, FE (or correlated RE) is needed.
3. `xtserial` (Stata, install via SSC): Wooldridge (2010) test for serial correlation in the idiosyncratic errors. If rejected, the standard RE/FE assumptions about $v_{it}$ may be violated.
4. Variable addition test (Wooldridge 1995): Tests for nonignorable selection bias in unbalanced panels.

The "non-switchers" issue with `xtlogit, fe`: Stata will print "obs dropped due to no variation" — if this is a large fraction of the sample, the FE logit estimates may be unrepresentative.

For cluster-robust standard errors in R: the `clubSandwich` package provides `vcovCR(model, cluster = df$id, type = "CR1S")` for cluster-robust variance estimation compatible with most model classes.
:::



# Synthesis and Open Frontiers {background-color="#1a2a4a"}

## Decision Flowchart

**Step 1 — What type of outcome?**

Binary → Blocks 2/3/6A | Ordered → Blocks 4/6B | Count → Blocks 5/6C | Censored → Block 8 | Selection → Block 9

. . .

**Step 2 — FE or RE?**

Run Mundlak test (`test xbar1 xbar2 ...`).
Reject $H_0$ → Use FE (or correlated RE) | Fail to reject → RE sufficient

. . .

**Step 3 — Is there temporal dependence?**

Run serial correlation test (`xtserial` / `pbgtest`).
Reject $H_0$ → Add lagged outcome; address initial conditions (Wooldridge 2005 device)

. . .

**Step 4 — Is the panel balanced?**

Unbalanced → Test ignorability of attrition (Wooldridge 1995 variable addition test).
Reject → Full selection correction (Block 9)

. . .

**Step 5 — Report average partial effects**, not raw coefficients. Use `margins` / `marginaleffects`.

::: {.notes}
This flowchart provides a practical decision guide for researchers. The key principle is to start with the simplest defensible specification and add complexity only when diagnostics demand it.

A common mistake is to jump directly to complex estimation procedures (dynamic FE ordered logit, Kyriazidou sample selection) without first verifying that the simpler models fail. If tests for individual effects, serial correlation, and selection bias all pass, the pooled estimator with cluster-robust standard errors may be sufficient.

The instruction to report average partial effects (APEs) rather than coefficients is especially important for nonlinear models: the coefficient $\hat{\beta}$ in a probit or Poisson model does not have a direct causal or policy interpretation without transformation. The APE, averaged over the empirical distribution of covariates, provides the natural analogue of the OLS coefficient in a linear model.
:::

## Open Frontiers and Current Developments

**Partial identification in FE models:**
Honoré & Tamer (2006) provide informative bounds on $\beta$ when point identification fails in FE binary choice. Extension to ordered and dynamic cases (Müller et al. 2021) is active research.

. . .

**Machine learning and high-dimensional fixed effects:**
`fixest` handles millions of observations and thousands of fixed effects. Current research explores regularisation (LASSO, ridge) for selecting controls while maintaining consistent $\hat{\beta}$ in panel GLMs.

. . .

**Bayesian panel GLMs:**
Hasegawa (2009) — Bayesian dynamic ordered probit via MCMC. Schnakenberg & Fariss (2014) — dynamic ordinal IRT. Particularly valuable for short panels ($T \leq 4$) where frequentist FE methods discard too much information.

. . .

**Non-rectangular panels and multiple imputation:**
Multiple imputation for missing panel data (Rubin 1987 extended to panel settings); pattern mixture models for MNAR data.

::: {.notes}
These open frontiers point to active research directions that students at the advanced PhD level may wish to pursue.

The partial identification approach (Honoré & Tamer 2006) is particularly promising for social science applications where identifying assumptions for point identification are implausible. Partial identification provides honest bounds on parameters rather than forcing point estimates that rest on questionable assumptions.

Machine learning methods for panel GLMs are developing rapidly. The `fixest` package already implements some of these, and the `DoubleML` package in R provides double/debiased ML estimators for panel data models with high-dimensional covariates.

For Bayesian methods: Hasegawa (2009) implements a Bayesian dynamic ordered probit model via MCMC that handles the initial conditions problem naturally through the prior on $\mu_i | y_{i0}$. This approach is particularly appealing for very short panels where the Wooldridge device may be imprecise.
:::

**Software documentation and packages:**

- **Stata:** `xtlogit`, `xtprobit`, `xtpoisson`, `xtnbreg`, `xttobit`, `xtoprobit` — *Stata 18 Longitudinal/Panel Data Reference Manual*. [stata.com](https://www.stata.com/manuals/xt.pdf)
- **R `fixest`:** Bergé, L. (2018). Efficient estimation of maximum likelihood models with multiple fixed-effects. *Econometrics Journal*, 21(3), 388–408. [doi:10.1111/ectj.12101](https://doi.org/10.1111/ectj.12101) | [Package](https://lrberge.github.io/fixest/)
- **R `lme4`:** Bates et al. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 67(1). [doi:10.18637/jss.v067.i01](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v067.i01) | [Package](https://cran.r-project.org/package=lme4)
- **R `ordinal`:** Christensen, R.H.B. (2019). ordinal — Regression models for ordinal data. [Package](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ordinal)
- **R `pglm`:** Croissant, Y. (2020). pglm: Panel generalised linear models. [Package](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pglm)
- **R `marginaleffects`:** Arel-Bundock et al. (2024). *Journal of Statistical Software*, 111(9). [doi:10.18637/jss.v111.i09](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v111.i09) | [Website](https://marginaleffects.com)
- **R `tscount`:** Liboschik et al. (2017). tscount: An R package for analysis of count time series following generalized linear models. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 82(5). [doi:10.18637/jss.v082.i05](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v082.i05) | [Package](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tscount)
- **R `censReg`:** Henningsen, A. (2010). Estimating censored regression models in R using the censReg package. [Package](https://cran.r-project.org/package=censReg)
- **R `clubSandwich`:** Pustejovsky, J.E. (2015). Cluster-robust variance estimation. [Package](https://cran.r-project.org/package=clubSandwich)
- **BUC estimator:** `ssc install buc` in Stata; code accompanying Baetschmann et al. (2015)
- **Honoré estimator:** `ssc install honor` in Stata; [author's page](https://www.princeton.edu/~honore/)
